title: Base of the Cambrian: Treptichnus pedum burrows

facts.text: A rock section at Fortune Head, Newfoundland, is the formal base of the Cambrian, traced worldwide by the first Treptichnus pedum burrows.
Treptichnus pedum is a burrow trace fossil linked to early priapulid worms; finds a few metres below the boundary led to using its whole trace assemblage.
Modern radiometric dating puts the boundary at 538.8 ± 0.6 Ma; in 2022 the age was revised from 541 Ma.
The boundary opens the Paleozoic Era and the Phanerozoic Eon, and now lies below the first trilobites and small shelly fossils.
Several chemical markers show a drastic change in the environment around the start of the Cambrian.
Beginning about 538.8 Ma, complex life diversified suddenly, producing the first representatives of most modern animal phyla.
The early Cambrian burst lasted about 20–25 million years; its high evolutionary rates had ended by 521 Ma, when trilobites appear.
Animals gained mineralised skeletons, more complex bodies and behaviour, and began burrowing, changing the sea floor and opening new ecosystems.
Molybdenum isotopes tie rising early Cambrian biodiversity to the spread of oxygenated bottom waters, supporting oxygen as a driver.
Its rate of diversification is unmatched among marine animals, though how explosive it really was is still debated.

title: First orthid brachiopods

facts.text: Orthida, an order of brachiopods, appeared in the Early Cambrian (Botomian) and became very diverse in Ordovician shelf seas.
They began to differentiate in the late Early Cambrian and had diversified into many forms, 2–5 cm wide, by the late Cambrian.
Orthids are the oldest members of the articulate brachiopods (Rhynchonelliformea) and the order from which all other brachiopods of this group stem.
Orthids were sessile filter feeders, often anchoring themselves onto firm substrates.

facts.text: Small shelly fossils, mineralized tubes, spicules and plates often only millimetres long, form a nearly continuous record from the latest Ediacaran to the end of the Early Cambrian.
Graham Budd's scheme runs from a Tube world (550–536 Ma) to a Sclerite world of halkieriids, tommotiids and hyoliths ending about 525 Ma.
Their fairly continuous record shows phyla appearing in a rapid but orderly sequence rather than a sudden jumble.
Signs of selective predator attacks on them suggest predation helped drive new species.
Most were thought wiped out in the end-Botomian extinction, but their apparent disappearance may partly reflect the loss of phosphate preservation.
A marine transgression began at the start of the Cambrian, and sea level rose gradually through the period.
It was the second-greatest sustained sea-level rise of the Phanerozoic, as the climate grew warmer.
Shallow seas spread across flat eroded surfaces such as the sub-Cambrian peneplain and the Great Unconformity, burying them under marine sediments.
Seas spread over Baltica and much of Antarctica, and marine invertebrates flourished in the shallow waters.
In North America this Sauk transgression began in earnest only in the middle Cambrian.
An asteroid about 1 km across struck what is now the Gulf of Finland, Estonia, around 535 Ma.
The Cambrian page describes a complex crater about 20 km wide with inner ridges; the Neugrund page gives 8 km.
It was once dated to the Ordovician, around 470 Ma, before newer research gave a Cambrian age.

title: Pampean orogeny on Gondwana's western margin

facts.text: The Pampean orogeny built mountains on the western margin of Gondwana during the Cambrian, between about 535 and 520 Ma.
It partly involved an exotic terrane accreted to Gondwana's proto-Pacific margin, long before the Andes formed.
A magmatic belt of its igneous rocks formed from 525 to 515 Ma.
Around 530 Ma, a block now part of Argentina rifted away from Laurentia and later joined Gondwana.
Rifting separated Cuyania from Laurentia's Ouachita embayment and opened a new ocean that widened into the Early Ordovician.
Paleomagnetic evidence supports Cuyania's Laurentian origin; it later accreted to Gondwana.

conflicts.date_text: towards the end of the early Cambrian
conflicts.note: Cambrian page places the rifting late in the early Cambrian

facts.text: The first known footprints on land date to about 530 Ma, though the evidence that arthropods were on land so early is unconfirmed.
Early Cambrian trace fossils suggest mollusc-like animals could spend at least 15 minutes on land.
Tracks from the Cambrian–Ordovician boundary, about 490 Ma, are read as large amphibious arthropods, perhaps euthycarcinoids, crossing coastal dunes.
Around 530 Ma the Kalahari and Mawson cratons joined in the Kuunga–Damara orogeny, completing southern Gondwana.
Deformation and metamorphism in the Damara orogeny peaked between 530 and 500 Ma.
Collisions in East Antarctica's Lützow-Holm and Prydz belts climaxed at 530 Ma.
A narrow ocean separated Amazonia from Gondwana until about 530 Ma; the last stages of assembly overlapped with the Cambrian explosion.
West Gondwana was stitched together along the Transbrasiliano lineament in the mid-Cambrian, as Amazonia collided with the São Francisco–Congo and Río de la Plata blocks.

facts.text: A positive carbon isotope excursion, the ZHUCE, coincides with the first appearances of the molluscs Watsonella crosbyi and Aldanella attleborensis around 529 Ma.
Together these markers reliably indicate the boundary between the Fortunian and Cambrian Stage 2.
Cambrian Stage 2 is the unnamed upper stage of the Terreneuvian Series, lying above the Fortunian and below Stage 3.

title: Early Cambrian oxygen pulses (CARE excursion)

facts.text: In Stages 2 and 3, linked carbon and sulphur isotope excursions record heavy burial of organic carbon and pyrite in productive but anoxic seafloor waters.
Oxygen-rich waters then spread from the deep ocean into shallow seas, extending the habitable seafloor.
These oxygen pulses match the radiation of small shelly fossils and the Cambrian arthropod radiation isotope excursion (CARE).
Oxygenation cut burial rates and anoxia returned; the cycle repeated several times in the early Cambrian.
Rising seawater 87Sr/86Sr shows stronger continental weathering, which fed nutrients to the oceans.

facts.text: The Timanide Orogen formed as Baltica and Arctida collided between 528 and 510 Ma.
Erosion of the mountain belt began in the Cambrian and grew stronger in the Ordovician.
Sediments eroded from the Timanide Orogen are found in the East European Platform, including the Cambrian Sablino Formation near Lake Ladoga.
Some researchers dissent from the collision view and suggest there was never such a collision.
Uranium–lead dating places the Ramgarh impact in India between 528 and 395 Ma; other studies propose a younger age.
In 1972 A. R. Crawford proposed an impact origin after finding shatter coned colluvium in the middle of the crater.
A 2020 study gave stronger evidence for an impact origin, and the Earth Impact Database then classified the structure as a confirmed hypervelocity impact crater.
The impact may have happened in a shallow-water environment, as soft-sediment deformation near the apparent rim and an overlying diamictite layer suggest.
Archaeocyaths, sessile cup-shaped sponges with porous calcareous skeletons, are first known from East Siberia at the start of the Tommotian, 525 Ma.
With cyanobacteria, they built the early Cambrian reefs in warm tropical seas, the oldest known large-scale structures made by animals.
They diversified rapidly in Stage 3, then declined sharply in Stage 4.

facts.text: Sirius Passet in Greenland, part of the Buen Formation, preserves a fauna like that of China's Maotianshan Shales.
Its animals were most likely preserved under a microbial-mat death mask.
It is one of the Cambrian's major Lagerstätten, with the Burgess Shale and Maotianshan Shales.
Trilobite body fossils first appear around 521 Ma, as trilobites evolved mineralised calcite exoskeletons.
Their first appearance is the proposed base of Cambrian Series 2 and Stage 3, and the top of the Terreneuvian.
Trace fossils such as Rusophycus and Cruziana, claimed as trilobite tracks, appear from about 537 Ma.
They quickly diversified into the typical Cambrian orders, Redlichiida, Ptychopariida, Agnostida and Corynexochida, becoming the most diverse early Cambrian animals.
Even the earliest trilobites had complex compound eyes with calcite lenses.

title: First eocrinoid echinoderms

facts.text: Eocrinoids, an extinct echinoderm class, first appear in Cambrian Stage 3 and lasted into the Silurian.
They were the earliest known stalked echinoderms with brachioles and the most common echinoderms of the Cambrian.

title: First radiodonts, the giant predators

facts.text: Radiodonts, an order of stem-group arthropods, appear in Cambrian Series 2 and thrived worldwide through the Cambrian.
Most were much larger than other Cambrian animals, with large species typically 30–50 cm long.
The radiodont Anomalocaris grew up to 2 m long, the largest animal in Cambrian seas.

facts.text: A confirmed impact crater about 2 km across at Ritland, Norway, formed about 520 ± 20 Ma.
The structure was first noticed as a suspected impact crater in 2000 by geologist Fridtjof Riis.
In 2008 microscopic evidence was announced: shocked quartz particles, which form only under the very high pressures of 5-10 GPa in a meteorite impact.
From about 520 to 450 Ma, Cambrian sediments in the Transantarctic Mountains were uplifted, folded, metamorphosed and intruded by granite batholiths.
After early Cambrian rifting, Antarctica deformed and the Transantarctic Mountains rose in the mid-Cambrian.
The Ross orogeny was one of the most extensive orogenic events in Antarctica, causing widespread plutonism and metamorphism.
Bimodal magmatism and extension marked the start of the orogeny; later, sedimentary rocks at the continental margin were deformed, metamorphosed and intruded with granite batholiths.
The Maotianshan Shales of Chengjiang, Yunnan, preserve an extremely diverse early Cambrian fauna with soft tissues, deposited no earlier than 518 Ma.
They hold the oldest diverse animal assemblage of the Phanerozoic, the best record of the Cambrian explosion.
Chengjiang has all the animal groups of the Burgess Shale but is about ten million years older, implying earlier or faster diversification.
Its chordates include Haikouella, Yunnanozoon and early fish such as Haikouichthys; its arthropods also occur elsewhere, suggesting a global range.
About one in eight of its animals are problematic forms of uncertain affinity.

facts.text: The earliest known vertebrates belong to China's Chengjiang biota, about 518 Ma; fish are thought to have begun evolving around 530 Ma.
Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia had fins, vertebrate muscles and gills; Haikouichthys had distinct vertebrae.
Chordates, including tunicates and vertebrates, diversified in the Cambrian as mid-sized suspension feeders in open water or near the bottom.
Metaspriggina, from the younger Burgess Shale about 505 Ma, had an elongate body, prominent eyes and gills.
Despite their later abundance, early vertebrates remain rare in the Cambrian record.

facts.text: Crustaceans had appeared by 517 Ma, in the Stage 3 Chengjiang biota, as relatives of living crustacean lineages.
Sunella, a possible early relative of ostracods, suggests modern pancrustaceans existed by 517 Ma.
Their Cambrian record is sparse despite an apparently early, hidden diversification.
Most major crustacean groups, branchiopods, maxillopods and malacostracans, appear before the end of the Cambrian.

title: Last Ediacaran-type frond organisms

facts.text: Petalonamids, frond-like animals typical of the Ediacaran biota, are dated from about 635 to 516 Ma.
The group is taken to include Stromatoveris from the lower Cambrian and, in a 2022 study, middle Cambrian Thaumaptilon.
Rare possible Ediacaran survivors occur as late as 510–500 Ma, but no Cambrian report is widely accepted.

contested_note: Whether any Ediacaran-type organisms survived into the Cambrian is disputed.

facts.text: South Australia's Emu Bay Shale, dated to Stage 4 about 514–512 Ma, preserves soft tissue mineralized as apatite or calcium carbonate.
It holds the oldest phosphatized muscle tissue and is younger than the Chengjiang and Sirius Passet Lagerstätten.
A 2023 study suggested the Emu Bay Shale is about 512 million years old, based on a correlation to a radiometric date of 511.87 ± 0.14 Ma in the contemporaneous Billy Creek Formation.
In 2011, paired compound eyes 2-3 centimetres long from the Emu Bay Shale were described and assigned to Anomalocaris.

conflicts.note: 2023 study correlating to a 511.87 ± 0.14 Ma date

facts.text: The Delamerian orogeny, about 514 to 490 Ma, ended deposition in the Adelaide Superbasin and folded and deformed its rocks.
Australia's eastern margin was inverted and became a subduction zone of the Palaeo-Pacific.
The event is called the Delamerian Orogeny after Delamere, a small town on the Fleurieu Peninsula where evidence for it was found.
Most rocks of the Kanmantoo Province were highly deformed and underwent moderate to high grade metamorphism during the Delamerian Orogeny.

title: Sinsk anoxic event and end-Botomian extinction

facts.text: The Sinsk Event, about 513.5 Ma, began the end-Botomian crisis of Stages 4 and 5; it was the Phanerozoic's first mass extinction, removing over 60% of animal species.
A major transgression brought anoxic deep water onto the shelves, spreading black shales; the nearly synchronous Kalkarindji eruptions probably drove warming and deoxygenation.
It devastated reef faunas, above all the reef-dominating archaeocyath sponges, along with halkieriids and much of the small shelly fauna.
Many stem groups of sponges, cnidarians, brachiopods and molluscs died out; mobile animals such as trilobites recovered fast, but diversity stayed low into the early Ordovician.
Deep-water communities, such as the later Huayuan biota, may have come through largely intact in refugia.

facts.text: Around 511 Ma, flood basalts of the Kalkarindji large igneous province began erupting in what is now Australia.
They covered over 2,100,000 km², making it one of the largest and the earliest large igneous province of the Phanerozoic.
Eruptions in Stage 4 and the early Miaolingian released carbon dioxide, methane and sulphur dioxide, driving rapid climate change and warmer seas.
These changes show up as three large, rapid carbon isotope excursions.
The timing suggests the eruptions helped cause the early to middle Cambrian mass extinction.

title: Blackberry Hill: animals walk onto tidal flats

facts.text: Blackberry Hill in Wisconsin preserves some of the oldest evidence of animals walking out of the sea onto land: large molluscs and euthycarcinoid arthropods.
The Protichnites trackways come from Blackberry Hill and the Potsdam Sandstone of Quebec.
Climactichnites, the largest Cambrian trace fossil, formed on sandy tidal flats around 510 Ma.
The Glikson crater in Western Australia is about 19 km across.
Nearby dolerite dated 508 ± 5 Ma suggests the impact is younger, probably Paleozoic.
The discovery of shatter cones and microscopic shock effects is reliable evidence for an impact origin.
A ring-shaped aeromagnetic anomaly at the site was probably caused by the impact disrupting a horizontal sill of magnetic igneous rock.

verification.title: Geology and age of the Glikson impact structure, Western Australia

facts.text: The Burgess Shale of British Columbia, about 508–505 Ma, preserves soft-bodied animals as thin dark carbon films.
One of the best-known Cambrian Lagerstätten, it preserves a key record of the Cambrian explosion.
Its biota includes strange arthropods like Opabinia, and Anomalocaris, the first great apex predator.
Metaspriggina, an early vertebrate with prominent eyes and gills, and medusa-stage jellyfish such as Burgessomedusa also occur there.

conflicts.note: Timeline pages and Opabinia page give 505 Ma

image.caption: Martin R. Smith, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts.text: At the Series 2–Miaolingian boundary, the first major trilobite extinction removed the olenellids, eodiscids and most redlichiids.
A carbon isotope event, ROECE, marks the boundary and coincides with the main phase of Kalkarindji volcanism.
Spain's Murero Lagerstätte records this end-Lower Cambrian extinction, the Valdemiedes event, in detail.
Surviving trilobite orders evolved larger tails and thicker cuticles, better resisting predators.

title: First conodonts

facts.text: Conodonts, eel-like jawless animals known mostly from their tooth elements, first appear in the Middle Cambrian.
They lasted more than 300 million years, from the Cambrian to the start of the Jurassic.
Conodonts are known mainly from hard, mineralised tooth-like structures called conodont elements, which in life sat in the oral cavity and were used to process food.
It has been proposed that conodonts may be stem-cyclostomes, more closely related to hagfish and lampreys than to jawed vertebrates.
Conodonts diversified extensively in the early Ordovician, reached their peak diversity in the middle of that period, and declined sharply in the late Ordovician and Silurian.

title: Paleo-Tethys Ocean begins to open

facts.text: The Paleo-Tethys Ocean began to open along Gondwana's northern margin in the Middle Cambrian.
It grew through the Paleozoic and closed in the Late Triassic, lasting about 400 million years.
Paleo-Tethys was a precursor to the Tethys Ocean (Neo-Tethys), which lay between Gondwana and the Hunic terranes, continental fragments that broke off Gondwana and moved north.
A last remnant of the Paleo-Tethys might be oceanic crust under the Black Sea.
The role of the Paleo-Tethys in the supercontinent cycle, especially the break-up of Pangaea, is unresolved.

title: Paradoxides, giant trilobites, spread worldwide

facts.text: Paradoxides, a genus of large to very large trilobites, lived throughout the world in the Middle Cambrian (Miaolingian).
They were the largest Cambrian trilobites.
One record-breaking specimen of Paradoxides davidis, described by John William Salter in 1863, is 37 cm long.
Like many early trilobites, Paradoxides had nonfulcrate thorax segments that allowed the animal to roll up.

facts.text: The Drumian carbon isotope excursion (DICE) marks the start of the Drumian age, about 504.5 Ma.
It was caused by anoxic deep waters rising into shallower settings as they transgressed.
DICE hampered the recovery of reef ecosystems already hit by the early-middle Cambrian mass extinctions.
The Dresbachian extinction event, about 502 Ma, was one of the Cambrian crises that preceded the Cambrian–Ordovician extinction.
Carbonate sequences such as those of the North China Craton record Cambrian extinction events like the biomeres.
Its page calls it the second of two severe Cambrian extinctions, after the end-Botomian; North America's Dresbachian stage spans 501 to 497 Ma.
A meteorite 200–300 m across struck Buskerud, Norway, about 500 ± 10 Ma, leaving the 5 km Gardnos crater.
Post-impact sediments show it hit a shallow sea; rock avalanches and debris flows followed when the crater rim was breached.
The site was first believed to be a volcanic crater, but in 1990 geologists Johan Naterstad and Johannes A. Dons confirmed it was formed by meteorite impact.
The impact fractured the bedrock and forced a powder of crushed rock into all the fractures, forming an impact breccia.
The 5 km Mizarai crater in Lithuania formed about 500 Ma.
The Mizarai crater is the second largest in Lithuania; it is not exposed at the surface, and the village of Mizarai now stands on the site.
Gediminas Motuza discovered the crater during the international Eurobridge seismic survey, which reached depths of 90-100 km.

facts.text: The 3.2 km Newporte structure in North Dakota formed about 500 Ma or slightly later.
Sweden's Kinnekulle Orsten and Alum Shale reveal the oldest well-documented seafloor meiofauna, including microscopic arthropods such as free-living pentastomids.
The Orsten fauna are fossilized organisms preserved in Cambrian rocks (Late Miaolingian to Furongian), notably at Kinnekulle and on the island of Oland in Sweden.
Konservat-Lagerstatten are deposits known for exceptional preservation of fossilized organisms or traces.
The 24 km Presqu'île crater in Quebec is estimated to be less than 500 million years old.

title: Onset of the Great Ordovician Biodiversification

facts.text: A Paleozoic-wide biodiversity study dates the start of the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event to 497.05 Ma, in the late Cambrian.
Its first phase, tied to plankton, began in the late Cambrian as invertebrate lineages invaded open waters and started new food chains.
Oxic waters expanded into deep and shelf seas in the latest Cambrian, as burrows deepened and body plans grew more complex.
Beginning in the mid-Guzhangian, an extinction cut species diversity by 45%; it ended early in the Furongian, perhaps mid-Paibian, about 3 million years later.
In South China it came in two phases: a slight decline over about 1.8 million years, then a sharper one over 1.2 million years.
Gradual ocean deoxygenation from the Guzhangian into the Jiangshanian, with the linked SPICE event, likely caused it; spreading anoxia killed off marjumiid and damesellid trilobites.
Shallow-water polymerid trilobites were replaced by deep-water olenimorph trilobites.
The onset of the SPICE excursion matches the extinction's second wave; diversity recovered at the very start of the Jiangshanian.

facts.text: The Steptoean positive carbon isotope excursion (SPICE) was a global event between about 497 and 494 Ma, starting near the Guzhangian–Paibian boundary.
Erosion of Gondwana's mountains pushed seawater 87Sr/86Sr to a peak, and spreading seafloor anoxia boosted burial of organic matter and pyrite.
Sea-level changes, cooling of surface water, anoxia and trilobite and brachiopod extinctions are all associated with it.
Its end matches the End-Steptoean biomere extinction.
The oxygen rise that followed opened niches for photosynthetic plankton and helped drive their radiation.

title: First cephalopods and nautiloids

facts.text: Plectronoceras, from the Late Cambrian, is the earliest undisputed cephalopod; its shell had septa and a siphuncle.
Nautiloids originated in the Late Cambrian and were already diverse in the Fengshan Formation of northeastern China, then a warm shallow sea.
The earliest nautiloids typically had ventral siphuncles, like later ammonites.

title: Jiangshanian extinction

facts.text: After diversity recovered at the start of the Jiangshanian, a new extinction cut species diversity by 55.2%.
It was followed by small fluctuations in species richness that lasted until shortly after the Ordovician began.
The Furongian is divided into the Paibian, the Jiangshanian and the unnamed 10th stage of the Cambrian.
The base of the Jiangshanian is marked by the first appearance of Agnostotes orientalis.

facts.text: The Famatinian orogeny ran from the Late Cambrian to at least the Late Devonian, with mountain building peaking about 490–460 Ma.
Plutonic rocks south of Chile's Salar de Atacama formed with it in the Cambrian and Ordovician.
A chain of volcanoes, the Famatinian magmatic arc, formed in what is now western South America.
The orogeny peaked when the Cuyania terrane collided with Pampia in the Ordovician.
From 480 to 435 Ma, rocks of the Cordillera Oriental were deformed as the arc developed.

conflicts.note: Famatinian orogeny: Cordillera Oriental deformed as the arc developed

facts.text: The Caledonian orogeny spans mountain-building events from the Ordovician to the Early Devonian, roughly 490–390 Ma.
Laurentia, Baltica and Avalonia collided, raising mountains now in northern Britain and Ireland, Scandinavia, Svalbard, East Greenland and north-central Europe.
Its onset has also been dated to about 500 Ma, in the Late Cambrian.
The Iapetus Ocean, widest in the Late Cambrian–Early Ordovician, began closing by subduction between 500 and 488 Ma.
In the Late Cambrian the Iapetus mid-ocean ridge subducted beneath Gondwana, opening large back-arc basins.

facts.text: The earliest brittle stars (ophiuroids) appear about 488 Ma.
The Ophiuroidea contain two large clades, Ophiurida (brittle stars) and Euryalida (basket stars).
Over 2,100 species of brittle stars in 256 recognized genera live today, making Ophiuroidea the most diverse and abundant echinoderm class.

title: Cambrian–Ordovician extinction event

facts.text: An extinction at the Cambrian–Ordovician boundary ended the Cambrian; another radiation followed that established the dominant Paleozoic animals.
It eliminated many brachiopods and conodonts and severely reduced the number of trilobite species.
Almost all Redlichiida and most Late Cambrian trilobite stocks died out, and agnostid diversity fell sharply.
Volcanism, especially from large igneous provinces, has been speculated as the cause of the crisis.
Some researchers argue the apparent extinction is an artifact of a gap in the rock record.

contested_note: Some researchers argue the extinction is an artifact of a gap in the stratigraphic record.
